edges: The demand for solid fats from liquid oils, from the margarine and soap industries, is what hydrogenation answered.
Ellis says the hardening of whale oil expanded its market and made Lever buy up rival hardening patents and firms.
Crisco applied hydrogenation, by Kayser’s route, to cottonseed oil.
Dyer shows the Crisco launch of 1911–1912 as the marketing of the new product.
The stern slipway of 1925 is the technology of the pelagic fleets of 1930–31.
Lever’s purchase of the world’s whale oil and the building of the pelagic fleets are the buying and supply sides of the same business.
Ellis says the war’s demand for glycerine raised the price of whale oil fourfold and the control of oil that Lever bought in 1919.
Ellis sets the 1931 convention and the 1937 amendments against the rising pelagic catches of the 1930s.
Ellis says the cost of the southern fleet pressed Lever Brothers into the merger with the Margarine Union of 1929.
The merged firm and the Dutch margarine makers were the buyers of the margarine fats whose mix changes.
Van Stuyvenberg ties the American soybean’s rise to margarine’s change of raw material, as Kiple describes the supply side.
American soy was tried after Manchurian soy had shown the crop’s potential, and expanded when the war cut other supplies.
Hunt ties the tariff chain at Ottawa and in France to the depression’s overproduction of oils and fats.
Rationing and import cut-offs sped margarine’s move to domestic cottonseed and soybean oil.
Van Stuyvenberg notes that the 1902 tax led manufacturers to use naturally yellow groundnut and soybean oils.
Van Stuyvenberg says the farm support of cotton and soy growers for margarine helped bring the 1949–50 repeal.
The plantations founded from 1911 are the Asian industry that overtook Nigeria in 1934.
Kiple says Lever’s refusal in British West Africa in 1907 is why he took his palm-oil plans to the Congo in 1911.
The plantings of 1911 and after are the hectares that Kiple counts in 1919–1938.
Kiple says the new Tenera planting material, bred after 1945, was what raised yields on the plantations that followed.
Hallet, rich from the Congo, carried his oil-palm experience from the Congo to Sumatra.
Teicholz traces the AHA’s 1961 advice to Keys’s hypothesis.
Kummerow’s trans-fat studies concern the hydrogenated fats Crisco had introduced.
The coconut plantations supplied the glycerine whose wartime value made whale oil contraband in the same war.
Lever’s Congo palm plantations and the Pacific coconut estates were the two tropical oil frontiers of the interwar years.
Unilever’s Indian vanaspati business and the 1929 merger of Lever and the Margarine Union are one company’s two ends.
Lever’s Solomon plantations are the best-documented case of the Pacific copra economy that the war for glycerine made strategic.
The Solomon Islands and the Congo are the only two Lever plantation companies before the 1920s.
Lever’s Nigerian soap works and its refusal of West African concessions are two sides of the company’s West African policy.
Nigeria’s groundnut exports and Southeast Asia’s overtaking of Nigeria in palm oil belong to the same interwar vegetable-oil market.
Turkey’s tariff and the Unilever survey show the company reading a market from Rotterdam.
